claim: Superficial neuromasts in larval zebrafish contain three cell classes organized in radial symmetry and a single planar-polarity axis.
source: We use the superficial neuromasts in larval zebrafish, which contain three cell classes organized in radial symmetry and a single planar-polarity axis.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by schematic diagrams in Figure 1A-C showing the three cell classes and their organization.

claim: Neuromasts regenerate isotropically to recover geometric order, proportions and polarity with exceptional accuracy.
source: Visualization of cell-fate transitions at high temporal resolution shows that neuromasts regenerate isotropically to recover geometric order, proportions and polarity with exceptional accuracy.
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data and quantitative analysis shown in Figures 3-4, demonstrating recovery of neuromast architecture after various injury regimes.

claim: Mediolateral position within the growing tissue is the best predictor of cell-fate acquisition during neuromast regeneration.
source: We identify mediolateral position within the growing tissue as the best predictor of cell-fate acquisition.
evidence: This is demonstrated through machine learning analysis in Figure 8, which identifies normalized distance to center and distance to mantle cells as the most predictive features.

claim: The neuromasts of the superficial lateral line in zebrafish are formed by a circular cuboidal epithelium of 60–70 cells.
source: The neuromasts of the superficial lateral line in zebrafish are formed by a circular cuboidal epithelium of 60–70 cells (López-Schier and Hudspeth, 2006; Ghysen and Dambly-Chaudière, 2007; Norden, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Mechanoreceptive hair cells occupy the center of the neuromast organ.
source: Mechanoreceptive hair cells occupy the center of the organ, whereas non-sensory sustentacular supporting cells are found around and between the hair cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A showing the spatial organization of cell types.

claim: Non-sensory sustentacular supporting cells are found around and between the hair cells.
source: Mechanoreceptive hair cells occupy the center of the organ, whereas non-sensory sustentacular supporting cells are found around and between the hair cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Mantle cells form the outer rim of the neuromast organ.
source: A second class of supporting cell called mantle cells forms the outer rim of the organ.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The invariant spatial distribution of three cell classes generates radial symmetry in neuromasts.
source: The invariant spatial distribution of these three cell classes generates a radial symmetry (Figure 1B) (Pinto-Teixeira et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation support and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Neuromasts have an axis of planar polarity defined by the orientation of the hair-cells' apical hair bundle.
source: Neuromasts also have an axis of planar polarity defined by the orientation of the hair-cells' apical hair bundle (Figure 1C) (Ghysen and Dambly-Chaudière, 2007; Wibowo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation support and illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: Neuromasts contain around 40 sustentacular cells, 8–10 mantle cells, and 14–16 hair cells.
source: In addition to this geometric organization, cell-class number and proportions are largely constant, with around 40 sustentacular, 8–10 mantle, and 14–16 hair cells.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section describing neuromast composition.

claim: Non-sensory cells in neuromasts can proliferate.
source: Non-sensory cells can proliferate, whereas the sensory hair cells are postmitotic (López-Schier and Hudspeth, 2006; Ma et al., 2008; Cruz et al., 2015; Pinto-Teixeira et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the text with multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Sensory hair cells in neuromasts are postmitotic.
source: Non-sensory cells can proliferate, whereas the sensory hair cells are postmitotic (López-Schier and Hudspeth, 2006; Ma et al., 2008; Cruz et al., 2015; Pinto-Teixeira et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the text with multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: A string of interneuromast cells connects each neuromast along the entire lateral-line system.
source: Finally, a string of interneuromast cells connects each neuromast along the entire lateral-line system (Figure 1A) (Ghysen and Dambly-Chaudière, 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation support and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Laser-targeted cells are rapidly eliminated from the neuromast epithelium with no detectable collateral damage.
source: Using Sox2:GFP 5 day-old zebrafish larvæ that ubiquitously express a nucleus-targeted red-fluorescent protein (H2B-RFP) (Figure 1K–L), we certified that laser-targeted cells are rapidly eliminated from the neuromast epithelium with no detectable collateral damage (Figure 1M–P and Video 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through time-lapse imaging in Figure 1M-P and Video 1 showing cell elimination without damage to neighboring cells.

claim: Complete elimination of a neuromast is irreversible in larval zebrafish.
source: These data indicate that in contrast to what occurs in embryos (Sánchez et al., 2016), the complete elimination of a neuromast is irreversible in larval zebrafish.
evidence: This is concluded from experiments showing that none of 22 completely ablated neuromasts regenerated after 7 days (Figure 2A-E), and confirmed with an independent marker (n=9, Figure 2F-J).

claim: Interneuromast cells do not proliferate after neuromast ablation in larval zebrafish.
source: Finally, incubation of Alpl:mCherry specimens with Bromodeoxy-Uridine (BrdU) to reveal the DNA synthesis that occurs prior to mitosis showed that interneuromast cells do not proliferate after neuromast ablation (Figure 2K–N) (Gratzner, 1982).
evidence: This is demonstrated through BrdU labeling experiments shown in Figure 2K-N.

claim: Ablation of the posterior half of the neuromast is followed by closure of the wound within 24 hours.
source: We found that ablation of the posterior half of the neuromast was followed by closure of the wound within 24 hr (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: Neuromasts regain normal cell-class spatial distribution at 3 days post-injury after posterior half ablation.
source: At 3 dpi, target neuromasts regained normal cell-class spatial distribution (n = 6) (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3D with sample size provided.

claim: Neuromasts recover approximately 70% of normal cell number at 7 days post-injury after posterior half ablation.
source: At 7 dpi, neuromasts recovered approximately 70% of the normal cell number (Figure 3E,Z).
evidence: This is stated in the text and quantified in Figure 3E and 3Z.

claim: There is no difference in speed and extent of regeneration after ablating the posterior half of neuromasts with or without flanking interneuromast cells.
source: We found no difference in speed and extent of regeneration after concurrently ablating the posterior half of neuromasts and flanking interneuromast cells (n = 5) (Figure 3F–J,Z).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 3F-J,Z comparing the two conditions.

claim: Ablation of the posterior or dorsal half of the neuromast epithelium results in identical regeneration outcome.
source: The ablation of the posterior or the dorsal half of the epithelium resulted in identical outcome, suggesting that neuromasts are symmetric in their regenerative capacity (n = 6) (Figure 3K–O,Z).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 3K-O,Z showing similar regeneration patterns.

claim: Neuromasts are symmetric in their regenerative capacity.
source: The ablation of the posterior or the dorsal half of the epithelium resulted in identical outcome, suggesting that neuromasts are symmetric in their regenerative capacity (n = 6) (Figure 3K–O,Z).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ablation of different halves (posterior vs dorsal) results in identical regeneration outcomes.

claim: Complete elimination of mantle cells is followed by their re-emergence 3 days post-injury.
source: The complete elimination of mantle cells was followed by their re-emergence 3 dpi (Figure 3Q–S), and the reconstitution of the outer rim of the neuromast 7 dpi (n = 15) (Figure 3T,Z).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 3Q-T,Z with sample size provided.

claim: The outer rim of the neuromast is reconstituted 7 days post-injury after complete mantle cell ablation.
source: The complete elimination of mantle cells was followed by their re-emergence 3 dpi (Figure 3Q–S), and the reconstitution of the outer rim of the neuromast 7 dpi (n = 15) (Figure 3T,Z).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 3T,Z.

claim: Simultaneous ablation of mantle cells and adjacent interneuromast cells leads to identical regeneration outcome as mantle cell ablation alone.
source: The simultaneous ablation of the mantle cells and the adjacent interneuromast cells led to identical outcome (n = 6) (Figure 3U–Z).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 3U-Z comparing the two conditions.

claim: Ablation of interneuromast cells on one side of a neuromast does not trigger proliferation of remaining interneuromast cells over 7 days.
source: The ablation of the interneuromast cells in fish co-expressing Sox2:GFP and Alpl:mCherry on one side of a neuromast (n = 12), or between two adjacent organs (n = 8) did not trigger the proliferation of the remaining interneuromast cells over a period of 7 days (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–J).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-J with sample sizes provided.

claim: Interneuromast cells are not essential for neuromast regeneration in larval zebrafish.
source: Because the complete ablation of mantle cells leaves intact the sustentacular-cell population, and the hair cells are postmitotic, these results yield three important and novel findings: (1) interneuromast cells are not essential for neuromast regeneration in larval zebrafish, although they may contribute to mantle cell regeneration
evidence: This is concluded from experiments showing that neuromasts can regenerate after ablation of mantle cells even when interneuromast cells are also removed.

claim: Interneuromast cells may contribute to mantle cell regeneration.
source: Because the complete ablation of mantle cells leaves intact the sustentacular-cell population, and the hair cells are postmitotic, these results yield three important and novel findings: (1) interneuromast cells are not essential for neuromast regeneration in larval zebrafish, although they may contribute to mantle cell regeneration
evidence: This is suggested by the observation that regenerated organs are smaller when interneuromast cells are ablated along with mantle cells.

claim: Sustentacular cells are tri-potent progenitors able to self-renew and to generate mantle and hair cells.
source: Because the complete ablation of mantle cells leaves intact the sustentacular-cell population, and the hair cells are postmitotic, these results yield three important and novel findings: (1) interneuromast cells are not essential for neuromast regeneration in larval zebrafish, although they may contribute to mantle cell regeneration; (2) neuromasts have isotropic regenerative capacity; (3) sustentacular cells are tri-potent progenitors able to self-renew and to generate mantle and hair cells.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that sustentacular cells can regenerate all three cell types (sustentacular, mantle, and hair cells) as shown in lineage tracing experiments in Figure 5.

claim: Neuromasts reduced to 4-10 cells can regenerate and recover approximately 70% of normal cell count at 7 days post-injury.
source: We found that after losing over 95% of their cellular content, neuromasts recover an average of 45 cells at 7 dpi (or approximately 70% of the normal cell count), with exceptional cases reaching 60 cells (equivalent to over 90% of a normal organ) (n = 15) (Figure 4K).
evidence: This is stated in the text and quantified in Figure 4K with sample size provided.

claim: Regenerating neuromasts become radial-symmetric as early as 3 days post-injury after severe ablation.
source: Regenerating neuromasts became radial-symmetric as early as 3 dpi (Figure 4D), and had normal cell-class composition and proportions 7 dpi (Figure 4L–M).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 4D showing radial symmetry recovery.

claim: Regenerating neuromasts have normal cell-class composition and proportions 7 days post-injury after severe ablation.
source: Regenerating neuromasts became radial-symmetric as early as 3 dpi (Figure 4D), and had normal cell-class composition and proportions 7 dpi (Figure 4L–M).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 4L-M showing cell-class proportions.

claim: During the first 24 hours post-injury, intact cells rebuild a circular epithelium.
source: During the first 24 hpi, the intact cells rebuilt a circular epithelium (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: From 1 to 3 days post-injury, cell number increases rapidly and proportion is restored during neuromast regeneration.
source: From 1 dpi to 3 dpi, cell number increases rapidly and proportion is restored (Figure 4C,K–M).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 4C,K-M showing cell number and proportion changes over time.

claim: After 3 days post-injury, cell number increases at a slower pace during neuromast regeneration.
source: After 3 dpi, cell number increases at a slower pace (Figure 4K–M).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 4K-M showing the rate of cell number increase over time.

claim: Each cell class assumes an appropriate position despite much reduced cell number during neuromast regeneration.
source: Importantly, each cell class assumes an appropriate position despite a much reduced cell number (Figure 4E,J,L–P).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 4E,J,L-P showing proper cell positioning even with reduced cell numbers.

claim: Regenerated neuromasts show correct apicobasal polarity with proper positioning of nuclei and adherens junctions.
source: We found correct positioning of these markers in the regenerated epithelium (n = 4), including the typical apicobasal constriction of the hair cells (Figure 4S–T).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 4S-T showing basal nuclei and apical N-cadherin enrichment.

claim: Regenerated neuromasts are plane-polarized with half of the hair cells coherently oriented in opposition to the other half.
source: To assess epithelial planar polarity, we looked at hair-bundle orientation using fluorescent phalloidin, which revealed that 7 dpi the regenerated neuromasts were plane-polarized in a manner indistinguishable from unperturbed organs, with half of the hair cells coherently oriented in opposition to the other half (n = 10) (Figure 4U–W).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 4U-W showing hair bundle orientation.

claim: In the absence of interneuromast cells, regenerating hair cells recover normal coherent planar polarity.
source: In the absence of interneuromast cells regenerating hair cells recovered normal coherent planar polarity (n = 16), suggesting the existence of alternative sources of polarizing cues (Figure 4Z).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 4X-Z showing planar polarity recovery after interneuromast cell ablation.

claim: As few as four supporting cells can initiate and sustain integral organ regeneration.
source: Collectively, these findings reveal that as few as four supporting cells can initiate and sustain integral organ regeneration.
evidence: This is concluded from experiments showing that neuromasts reduced to 4-10 cells can fully regenerate with proper architecture, proportions, and polarity.

claim: The majority of founder sustentacular cells undergo three divisions during regeneration.
source: We found that the majority of the founder sustentacular cells underwent three divisions and that some divided up to five times (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 5D showing division rounds.

claim: 14 out of 30 founder mantle cells do not divide during regeneration.
source: 14 out of 30 founder mantle cells did not divide at all, and the rest divided once or, rarely, twice.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on cell tracking data from 30 founder mantle cells.

claim: Founder sustentacular cells require on average 19 ± 6 hours to divide.
source: Founder sustentacular cells required on average 19 ± 6 hr (mean ±s.d., n = 76) to divide, whereas the founder mantle cells that divided required on average 27 ± 5 hr, (mean ±s.d., n = 30) (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is stated in the text with statistical measures and sample sizes, and shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Founder mantle cells that divide require on average 27 ± 5 hours to divide.
source: Founder sustentacular cells required on average 19 ± 6 hr (mean ±s.d., n = 76) to divide, whereas the founder mantle cells that divided required on average 27 ± 5 hr, (mean ±s.d., n = 30) (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is stated in the text with statistical measures and sample sizes, and shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Founder sustentacular cells produce all three cell classes (sustentacular, mantle and hair cells).
source: Clones from founder sustentacular and founder mantle cells were markedly different: founder sustentacular cells produced all three cell classes (sustentacular, mantle and hair cells), whereas founder mantle cells produced clones containing only mantle cells (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 5F showing clone composition.

claim: Founder mantle cells produce clones containing only mantle cells.
source: Clones from founder sustentacular and founder mantle cells were markedly different: founder sustentacular cells produced all three cell classes (sustentacular, mantle and hair cells), whereas founder mantle cells produced clones containing only mantle cells (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 5F showing clone composition.

claim: 97% of sustentacular-cell divisions are symmetric.
source: This analysis revealed that 97% of the sustentacular-cell divisions were symmetric: 78% produced two sustentacular cells (SS), 16% produced a pair of hair cells (HH), and 3% generated two mantle cells (MM).
evidence: This is stated in the text based on analysis of 307 sustentacular-cell divisions shown in Figure 5G.

claim: 78% of sustentacular-cell divisions produce two sustentacular cells.
source: This analysis revealed that 97% of the sustentacular-cell divisions were symmetric: 78% produced two sustentacular cells (SS), 16% produced a pair of hair cells (HH), and 3% generated two mantle cells (MM).
evidence: This is stated in the text based on analysis of 307 sustentacular-cell divisions shown in Figure 5G.

claim: 16% of sustentacular-cell divisions produce a pair of hair cells.
source: This analysis revealed that 97% of the sustentacular-cell divisions were symmetric: 78% produced two sustentacular cells (SS), 16% produced a pair of hair cells (HH), and 3% generated two mantle cells (MM).
evidence: This is stated in the text based on analysis of 307 sustentacular-cell divisions shown in Figure 5G.

claim: 3% of sustentacular-cell divisions generate two mantle cells.
source: This analysis revealed that 97% of the sustentacular-cell divisions were symmetric: 78% produced two sustentacular cells (SS), 16% produced a pair of hair cells (HH), and 3% generated two mantle cells (MM).
evidence: This is stated in the text based on analysis of 307 sustentacular-cell divisions shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Only 3% of sustentacular-cell divisions are asymmetric, generating one sustentacular and one mantle cell.
source: Only 3% of the divisions were asymmetric, generating one sustentacular and one mantle cell (SM) (n = 307).
evidence: This is stated in the text based on analysis of 307 sustentacular-cell divisions.

claim: All mantle-cell divisions are symmetric.
source: All mantle-cell divisions were symmetric (MM) (n = 20).
evidence: This is stated in the text based on analysis of 20 mantle-cell divisions shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Proliferation is markedly isotropic during the first 60 hours of neuromast regeneration.
source: We first assessed the spatial distribution of cell divisions during the first 60 hr of regeneration and found no pattern that would suggest regeneration anisotropy (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 6A showing even distribution of divisions across all quarters.

claim: 60 hours post-injury, most divisions (74%) take place in the dorsal and ventral (polar) quarters.
source: However, 60 hpi, most divisions (74%) took place in the dorsal and ventral (polar) quarters (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 6B showing spatial distribution of divisions.

claim: 60% of the progeny of anterior-localized founder cells are located in the anterior side of the resulting epithelium.
source: We found that 60% of the progeny of anterior-localized founder cells were located in the anterior side of the resulting epithelium, whereas 64% of the progeny of posterior-located founder cells were found in the posterior side (Figure 6C–E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 6C-E showing spatial distribution of progeny.

claim: 64% of the progeny of posterior-located founder cells are found in the posterior side of the resulting epithelium.
source: We found that 60% of the progeny of anterior-localized founder cells were located in the anterior side of the resulting epithelium, whereas 64% of the progeny of posterior-located founder cells were found in the posterior side (Figure 6C–E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 6C-E showing spatial distribution of progeny.

claim: 72% of cells derived from dorsal founder cells are located on the same side of the virtual dorsal/ventral midline.
source: We also found that 72% of cells derived from dorsal founder cells and 74% of cells from ventral founder cells were located on the same side of the virtual dorsal/ventral midline (Figure 6F–H).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 6F-H showing spatial distribution of progeny.

claim: 74% of cells from ventral founder cells are located on the same side of the virtual dorsal/ventral midline.
source: We also found that 72% of cells derived from dorsal founder cells and 74% of cells from ventral founder cells were located on the same side of the virtual dorsal/ventral midline (Figure 6F–H).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 6F-H showing spatial distribution of progeny.

claim: Most clones remain ipsilateral to the founder cell during neuromast regeneration.
source: Therefore, most of the clones remain ipsilateral to the founder cell.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that 60-74% of progeny remain on the same side as their founder cells.

claim: Neuromasts have isotropic regenerative capacity and their territorialization occurs by location-adaptive cellular differentiation.
source: These results indicate that neuromasts have isotropic regenerative capacity and their territorialization occurs by location-adaptive cellular differentiation.
evidence: This is concluded from observations showing isotropic proliferation early in regeneration and that clones tend to remain ipsilateral to founder cells rather than migrating.

claim: There are four types of clones from founder sustentacular cells: S (only sustentacular cells), SM (sustentacular and mantle cells), SH (sustentacular and hair cells), and SHM (all three cell classes).
source: We found four types of clones: containing only sustentacular cells (S), sustentacular and mantle cells (SM), sustentacular and hair cells (SH), and all three cell classes (SHM) (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 6I showing different clone types.

claim: 37 out of 72 clones from founder sustentacular cells are SH type.
source: We observed that 37/72 of the clones from founder sustentacular cells were SH, 21/72 were S, 12/72 were SM, and 2/72 were SHM (Figure 6I–K).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6I-K.

claim: 21 out of 72 clones from founder sustentacular cells are S type.
source: We observed that 37/72 of the clones from founder sustentacular cells were SH, 21/72 were S, 12/72 were SM, and 2/72 were SHM (Figure 6I–K).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6I-K.

claim: 12 out of 72 clones from founder sustentacular cells are SM type.
source: We observed that 37/72 of the clones from founder sustentacular cells were SH, 21/72 were S, 12/72 were SM, and 2/72 were SHM (Figure 6I–K).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6I-K.

claim: 2 out of 72 clones from founder sustentacular cells are SHM type.
source: We observed that 37/72 of the clones from founder sustentacular cells were SH, 21/72 were S, 12/72 were SM, and 2/72 were SHM (Figure 6I–K).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6I-K.

claim: There are three clear waves of cell divisions during neuromast regeneration, each spaced by 8-10 hours.
source: We found three clear waves of cell divisions, each spaced by 8–10 hr (Figure 7A), respectively peaking at 20 hr, 28 hr and 38 hr (Figure 7B–C)
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 7A-C showing temporal distribution of divisions.

claim: Cell division waves peak at 20 hours, 28 hours, and 38 hours post-injury.
source: We found three clear waves of cell divisions, each spaced by 8–10 hr (Figure 7A), respectively peaking at 20 hr, 28 hr and 38 hr (Figure 7B–C)
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 7B-C showing peaks in division frequency.

claim: Cell-cycle length in the 1st generation peaks around 10 hours (9.8 ± 3.3 hours, median ± interquartile range).
source: Cell-cycle length in the 1 st generation peaks around 10 hr (9.8 ± 3.3 hr, median ±interquartile range (iqr)) (Figure 7C)
evidence: This is stated in the text with statistical measures and shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Cell-cycle length in the 2nd generation is 11.5 ± 7.3 hours (median ± interquartile range).
source: but it begins to increase and to vary in the 2nd generation (11.5 ± 7.3 hr, median ±iqr)
evidence: This is stated in the text with statistical measures.

claim: Cell-cycle length in the 3rd generation is 18.8 ± 20.3 hours (median ± interquartile range).
source: and more so in the 3rd generation (18.8 ± 20.3 hr, median ±iqr).
evidence: This is stated in the text with statistical measures.

claim: Cell-cycle length is initially around 11 ± 3 hours and slowly increases up to 47 hours post-injury.
source: We found that the length of cell cycles is initially around 11 ± 3 hr (mean ±s.d.) and slowly increases up to 47 hpi.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on two-segment regression model analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: After 47 hours post-injury, cell-cycle length increases more rapidly and is more variable.
source: Afterwards, cell-cycle length increases more rapidly and is more variable (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 7D showing change in cell-cycle length over time.

claim: Above 24 cells, cell-cycle lengths show large variation.
source: Above this threshold, cell-cycles lengths show large variation.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on analysis shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The length of the cell cycle or the proliferative potential of founder sustentacular cells cannot explain clone composition.
source: With these data, we plotted proliferation kinetics against clone type, and found no significant difference between clones (Figure 7F–G). Thus, the length of the cell cycle or the proliferative potential of founder sustentacular cells cannot explain clone composition.
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 7F-G showing no significant differences in proliferation kinetics between clone types.

claim: The random forest algorithm was chosen as the best performing machine learning method with 83.1% accuracy.
source: In a pre-analysis, we compared the performance of 20 algorithms (support vector machines, decision trees and nearest neighbor classifiers) in terms of accuracy and area under the curve (AUC) and chose the ensemble bagged tree random forest algorithm (Breiman, 2001) as the best performing method (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 8—figure supplement 1 comparing different algorithms.

claim: SH vs. SM clones can be predicted with high accuracy (MCC = 0.63 ± 0.09) using machine learning.
source: Using machine learning, we were able to predict the occurrence of SH vs. SM clones from a founder sustentacular cell with high accuracy (42 out of 49 correctly predicted clones, MCC = 0.63 ± 0.09, mean ± s.d., n = 15 bootstrapped samples)
evidence: This is stated in the text with statistical measures and sample sizes, and shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Neither SH nor SM clones can be discriminated when compared to S clones using machine learning.
source: while neither SH nor SM clones could be discriminated when compared to S clones (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 8B showing low MCC values for these comparisons.

claim: Distance to the center of the epithelium and distance to mantle cells best discriminate SH vs SM clones.
source: Of the 32 features that we used, those that best discriminated SH vs SM clones were the sustentacular cells' distance to the center of the epithelium, and the distance to the mantle cells (Figure 8C and Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 8C and Figure 8—figure supplement 2 showing feature importance.

claim: HH and SM/MM divisions are highly predictable (MCC = 0.91 ± 0.07) using machine learning.
source: The HH and SM/MM divisions were highly predictable (63 out of 66 divisions correctly predicted, MCC = 0.91 ± 0.07, mean ± s.d., n = 15 bootstrapped samples)
evidence: This is stated in the text with statistical measures and sample sizes, and shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Discrimination between SS and HH or SM/MM divisions is much less accurate using machine learning.
source: while the discrimination between SS and HH or SM/MM divisions was much less accurate (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 8D showing lower MCC values for these comparisons.

claim: Distance to the neuromast center and distance to mantle cells are the most informative features for predicting division types.
source: Again, the most informative features were the distance to the neuromast center and the distance to the mantle cells (Figure 8E, Figure 8—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 8E and Figure 8—figure supplement 3 showing feature importance.

claim: SM/MM divisions occur consistently at the outer perimeter of the neuromast.
source: SM/MM divisions occur consistently at the outer perimeter of the neuromast (Figure 8F)
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 8F showing spatial distribution of division types.

claim: HH divisions take place near the center of the neuromast.
source: whereas HH divisions take place near the center.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 8F.

claim: Self-renewing SS divisions occupy the area between HH and SM/MM divisions.
source: Self-renewing SS divisions occupy the area between HH and SM/MM divisions.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 8F.

claim: SM/MM divisions are never seen in the anterior-most region of the neuromast.
source: Interestingly, SM/MM divisions were never seen in the anterior-most region of the organ
evidence: This is stated in the text based on spatial analysis of division locations shown in Figure 8F.

claim: Progenitor sustentacular cells are routed into generating mantle cells specifically in perimetral areas that lack mantle cells but not elsewhere.
source: suggesting that progenitor sustentacular cells are routed into generating mantle cells specifically in the perimetral areas that lack mantle cells but not elsewhere.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that SM/MM divisions occur at the periphery where mantle cells are needed but not in the anterior region.

claim: Regenerating neuromasts sense cell-class composition and route cellular differentiation in a spatially regulated manner to regain cell-class proportion and distribution.
source: Therefore, regenerating neuromasts appear to sense cell-class composition and route cellular differentiation in a spatially regulated manner to regain cell-class proportion and distribution.
evidence: This is concluded from observations showing that cell-fate decisions depend on position and local cellular environment.

claim: Neuromast regeneration begins immediately after injury with surviving founder cells reconstituting an epithelium.
source: By systematically analyzing cellular behavior, we reveal a hierarchical regenerative process that begins immediately after injury. First, surviving founder cells reconstitute an epithelium.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion summarizing findings from the time-lapse data.

claim: Sustentacular cells become proliferative and restore organ size during neuromast regeneration.
source: Second, sustentacular cells become proliferative and restore organ size.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion summarizing findings from the lineage tracing data.

claim: Cellular intercalation is rare during neuromast regeneration.
source: Cellular intercalation is rare.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on observations from cell tracking data showing that clones remain largely ipsilateral.

claim: Daughter cells differentiate in a position-appropriate manner to recreate cell-class proportions and organ geometric order during neuromast regeneration.
source: Third, daughter cells differentiate in a position-appropriate manner to recreate cell-class proportions and organ geometric order.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion summarizing findings from the machine learning analysis.

claim: The epithelium returns to a homeostatic state characterized by low mitotic rate after neuromast regeneration.
source: Fourth, the epithelium returns to a homeostatic state that is characterized by low mitotic rate.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on observations of cell-cycle lengthening over time shown in Figure 7.

claim: Neuromasts preferentially regenerate the cells that have been eliminated.
source: The milder damage regimes that eliminated one half of the epithelium show that neuromasts are symmetric in their regenerative capacity, and that they preferentially regenerate the cells that have been eliminated.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on observations from partial ablation experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: Neuromasts do not contain specialized cells that contribute dominantly to repair.
source: An important corollary of these results is that neuromasts do not contain specialized cells that contribute dominantly to repair.
evidence: This is concluded from observations showing that any sustentacular cell can act as a progenitor during regeneration.

claim: Progenitor behavior is a facultative status that every sustentacular cell can acquire or abandon during regeneration.
source: We propose that progenitor behavior is a facultative status that every sustentacular cell can acquire or abandon during regeneration.
evidence: This is proposed based on observations that sustentacular cells show variable proliferative behavior and clone composition.

claim: There is no regenerative overshoot of any cell class during neuromast regeneration.
source: We did not observe regenerative overshoot of any cell class (Agarwala et al., 2015)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on quantitative analysis of cell numbers and proportions over time.

claim: A mechanism exists that senses the total number of cells and the cell-class balance during tissue repair.
source: suggesting the existence of a mechanism that senses the total number of cells and the cell-class balance during tissue repair (Simon et al., 2009).
evidence: This is suggested based on the observation that cell-class proportions are accurately restored without overshoot.

claim: The mechanism controlling cell number and balance during neuromast regeneration may be based on the interplay between Fgf, Notch and Wnt signaling.
source: Together with previous work, our results support the possibility that such mechanism is based on the interplay between Fgf, Notch and Wnt signaling (Ma et al., 2008; Wibowo et al., 2011; Wada et al., 2013; Romero-Carvajal et al., 2015; Dalle Nogare and Chitnis, 2017).
evidence: This is suggested based on integration of current findings with previous literature on signaling pathways.

claim: Machine learning and quantitative videomicroscopy show clear differences between sustentacular and mantle cells.
source: Our combination of machine learning and quantitative videomicroscopy shows clear differences between sustentacular and mantle cells
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on the lineage tracing and machine learning analysis.

claim: Machine learning and quantitative videomicroscopy do not indicate heterogeneity within the sustentacular-cell population.
source: but does not indicate heterogeneity within the sustentacular-cell population.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on the inability to predict S vs SH or SM clones.

claim: Mantle cells can proliferate and generate a new primordium that migrates to produce new neuromasts after tail-fin amputation.
source: Complete elimination of parts of the lateral line by tail-fin amputation have revealed that mantle cells are able to proliferate and generate a new primordium that migrates into the regenerated fin to produce new neuromasts (Dufourcq et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion citing previous work.

claim: Mantle cells up-regulate the expression of multiple genes following neuromast injury.
source: Transcriptomic profiling of mantle cells following neuromast injury revealed that these cells up-regulate the expression of multiple genes (Steiner et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion citing previous work.

claim: Mantle cells constitute a quiescent pool of cells that re-enters cell cycle only in response to severe depletion of sustentacular cells.
source: Furthermore, a recent study has revealed that mantle cells constitute a quiescent pool of cells that re-enters cell cycle only in response to severe depletion of sustentacular cells (Romero-Carvajal et al., 2015)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion citing previous work.

claim: Mantle cells may conform a stem-cell niche for proliferation of sustentacular cells.
source: suggesting that these cells may conform a stem-cell niche for proliferation of sustentacular cells.
evidence: This is suggested in the Discussion based on previous findings about mantle cell behavior.

claim: Mantle cells may drive the regeneration of an entire neuromast if every other cell class is lost.
source: Thus, the collective evidence indicates that the mantle cells respond to damage and contribute to the regenerative processes, and may drive the regeneration of an entire organ if every other cell class is lost.
evidence: This is suggested in the Discussion based on integration of current and previous findings.

claim: The invariant radial symmetry of the neuromast serves as a rheostat to identify the site of damage to guide regeneration spatially.
source: We suggest a model in which the invariant radial symmetry of the neuromast serves as a rheostat to identify the site of damage to guide regeneration spatially (Figure 9).
evidence: This is proposed as a model in the Discussion and illustrated in Figure 9.

claim: A polarized axis along structurally intact and injured areas underlies the spatial guidance of neuromast regeneration.
source: A polarized axis along structurally intact and injured areas underlies this process.
evidence: This is proposed as part of the model in the Discussion.

claim: Partial maintenance of radial symmetry is not essential for neuromast regeneration.
source: However, the complete reconstruction of a neuromast by as few as 4 cells suggests that a partial maintenance of radial symmetry is not essential for organ regeneration.
evidence: This is concluded from observations that neuromasts can regenerate from very few cells that do not maintain radial symmetry.

claim: Radial-symmetry maintenance cannot have a deterministic impact on the recovery of geometric order during neuromast regeneration.
source: Therefore, radial-symmetry maintenance cannot have a deterministic impact on the recovery of geometric order.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that neuromasts can regenerate without maintaining radial symmetry.

claim: Partial structural maintenance and polarized tissue responses may optimize neuromast repair.
source: Yet, partial structural maintenance and polarized tissue responses may optimize repair, respectively, by preventing superfluous cellular production in undamaged areas and by biasing the production of lost cells in the damaged areas.
evidence: This is suggested in the Discussion based on observations of spatially biased regeneration.

claim: As few as four founder supporting cells can re-organize the local coherent planar polarity of the epithelium during neuromast repair.
source: This startling result indicates that as few as four founder supporting cells can re-organize the local coherent planar polarity of the epithelium during neuromast repair.
evidence: This is concluded from observations that neuromasts regenerated from 4-10 cells show proper planar polarity.

claim: Emx2 is expressed in one half of the hair cells of the neuromast (those oriented towards the tail) and absent in the other half (oriented towards the head).
source: Emx2 is expressed in one half of the hair cells of the neuromast (those oriented towards the tail) and absent in the other half (which are coherently oriented towards the head).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion citing recent work on Emx2.

claim: Loss of Emx2 leads to neuromasts with every hair cell pointing towards the head of the animal.
source: Loss- and gain-of-function of Emx2 alter planar cell polarity in a predictable manner: loss of Emx2 leads to neuromasts with every hair cells pointing towards the head of the animal
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion citing work on Emx2 function.

claim: Broad expression of Emx2 orients hair cells towards the tail of the animal.
source: and Emx2 broad expression orients hair cells towards its tail.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion citing work on Emx2 function.

claim: Emx2 may act in hair cells as a decoder of global polarity cues.
source: Because the coherent local axis of polarity is not affected by these genetic perturbations, Emx2 may act in hair cells as a decoder of global polarity cues.
evidence: This is suggested in the Discussion based on the effects of Emx2 manipulation on planar polarity.

claim: During neuromast regeneration, founder cells autonomously organize the variegated expression of Emx2 in the regrowing epithelium with consequent recovery of a coherent axis of planar polarity.
source: This evidence, together with our results, suggests that during neuromast regeneration founder cells autonomously organize the variegated expression of Emx2 in the regrowing epithelium with consequent recovery of a coherent axis of planar polarity and with one half of the hair cells pointing opposite to the other half.
evidence: This is suggested in the Discussion integrating current findings with knowledge about Emx2.

claim: Local coherent polarity in neuromasts is self-organizing.
source: Therefore, at present we can only support the notion that local coherent polarity is self-organizing
evidence: This is concluded from observations that neuromasts can recover planar polarity without interneuromast cells.

claim: Global orientation of neuromast planar polarity may be controlled externally.
source: whereas global orientation may be controlled externally.
evidence: This is suggested in the Discussion as a possibility that requires further testing.

claim: Local and global polarization of neuromasts occur independently of innervation.
source: Previous work has demonstrated that local and global polarization occur independently of innervation (López-Schier and Hudspeth, 2006)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion citing previous work.

claim: Intact resident cells can rapidly recreate their original microenvironment to rebuild a neuromast with normal organization, proportions and polarity.
source: The reduction of neuromasts to around 5% of their original size shows that intact resident cells can rapidly recreate their original microenvironment to rebuild a neuromast with normal organization, proportions and polarity.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion summarizing key findings.

claim: The extracellular matrix that remains intact after cell loss may serve as a blueprint for epithelial organization during neuromast regeneration.
source: Although these observations suggest autonomy, extrinsic sources of information including the extracellular matrix that remains intact after cell loss may serve as a blueprint for epithelial organization.
evidence: This is suggested in the Discussion as an alternative explanation for regeneration patterns.

claim: Cell-fate acquisition and cell-class distribution must be tissue-size dependent during neuromast regeneration.
source: Yet, unless such patterns are rebuilt together with the organ, neuromasts architecture and proportions would depend on the area occupied by the regrowing epithelium. In other words, cell-fate acquisition and cell-class distribution must be tissue-size dependent.
evidence: This is logically inferred from the discussion of how patterns could guide regeneration.

claim: Neuromasts regain geometric order when their cellular content is less than 60% of the original.
source: However, we show that neuromast regain geometric order as early as 2 days after injury, when their cellular content is less than 60% of the original.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on quantitative analysis of regeneration shown in Figure 4.

claim: Self-organization is an optimal morphogenetic process to govern organ repair because it requires the least amount of previous information and is robust to run-off signals.
source: We argue that self-organization is an optimal morphogenetic process to govern organ repair because (i) it requires the least amount of previous information and (ii) it is robust to run-off signals that could lead to catastrophic failure.
evidence: This is argued in the Discussion based on theoretical considerations.
